nodes.ask: Heat, cold, water, a current, an animal, altitude or a dive. First moves?
options: Airway, breathing and a central pulse; core temperature on a low-reading probe; glucose, ECG
Airway, breathing and pulse; a tympanic or temporal reading, which is fast and accurate enough here
Airway, breathing and pulse; acetaminophen for a high reading while the bloods are being sent
Airway, breathing and pulse; an oral thermometer reading, then warm or cool to that number
nodes.chainStep: Check airway, breathing and a central pulse (feel for 30 to 60 seconds in a cold patient); core temperature by esophageal, bladder or rectal probe, or a thermistor epitympanic probe, on a thermometer that reads below 35 °C; fingerstick glucose; cardiac monitor and 12-lead ECG; what happened: heat, cold, water, a current, an animal, altitude or a dive
nodes.why: Management turns on the core temperature, so it is measured close to the core with a thermometer that reads below 35 °C. Oral, axillary, temporal and infrared tympanic readings are not accurate in hypothermia, and after exercise in the heat only a rectal temperature is valid; most oral thermometers cannot read under 35 °C at all. In a cold patient the pulse is felt for longer (60 seconds in Paal 2022, 30 seconds in StatPearls), because it can be slow and faint. Antipyretics have no role in heat illness and may harm the liver and clotting. Glucose comes early, because hypoglycemia is common in heat illness and can cause or accompany hypothermia, and every hypothermic or electrically injured adult gets an ECG.

orders.dose: Esophageal, bladder or rectal probe, or a thermistor epitympanic probe; skin, temporal, oral, axillary and infrared tympanic readings are not accurate in hypothermia

orders.item: Core temperature, after exertion in the heat
orders.dose: Rectal temperature is the gold standard; oral, axillary, tympanic, forehead and temporal readings are not valid
Paal 2022: feel for vital signs for 60 seconds
orders.note: StatPearls Drowning extends the pulse check to 30 seconds in hypothermic patients.

orders.dose: Every patient with hypothermia and every adult after an electrical injury, with cardiac monitoring
Fingerstick early: hypoglycemia is frequent in heat illness and is on the list of causes behind hypothermia
No role; they may cause hepatic toxicity and worsen coagulopathy

nodes.note: Not in this version: thermal burns (the burns pathway, pw_burns, once it ships; smoke and cyanide are in pw_tox), carbon monoxide (pw_headache), avalanche burial, marine envenomation, bee and wasp stings beyond anaphylaxis, tick paralysis (pw_weakness), and children beyond the cases shown.

nodes.summary: Anaphylaxis after a sting or bite: IM epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh now, repeated every 5 to 15 minutes as needed, with early intubation if the airway is threatened, because it can be lost within minutes. The dyspnea pathway (pw_dyspnea) carries the anaphylaxis route, its weight-based dose and the observation afterwards.

Injured as well as exposed: the major trauma pathway (pw_trauma) takes it from here, with spinal immobilization for a dive into shallow water or a fall. Keep stripping wet clothing and insulating, because hypothermia worsens trauma coagulopathy, and return to this pathway for the exposure once the primary survey is done.

nodes.ask: Cold, pulseless on a full pulse check, core under 30 °C, no sign of death. Next?
options: Continuous CPR, shocks for VF, and ECLS rewarming; resuscitation goes on until warm
Standard ALS, stopping after 30 minutes without ROSC, as for any normothermic arrest
No CPR, as fixed dilated pupils and stiff limbs mean the patient has died
Rewarm with forced air first, and start CPR once the core is back over 30 °C
nodes.chainStep: Continuous CPR (mechanical device for prolonged CPR or transport); defibrillate VF (Paal 2022: if 3 shocks fail below 30 °C, wait until the core is over 30 °C, and hold epinephrine and amiodarone below 30 °C; the Korean 2025 guideline uses standard ALS); transfer for ECLS (VA ECMO) rewarming; HOPE score to guide ECLS; warmed IV fluids; check potassium
nodes.why: Hypothermic arrest is treated differently from normothermic arrest, and good neurological recovery is possible after long resuscitations when the cold came first. Compressions and ventilation are standard and run continuously until ROSC, and the guidelines keep resuscitating until the patient is warm, judging termination at the target temperature rather than after a fixed time. VF is shocked; how many shocks and whether to give epinephrine below 30 °C differs between the sources (see the orders). Rewarming is by ECLS, preferably VA ECMO. Asystole, an unwitnessed arrest, a very low core temperature, fixed dilated pupils and apparent rigor mortis are not, in Paal 2022, reasons to withhold rewarming, and rewarming before CPR would leave the patient without compressions.

orders.dose: As for a normothermic arrest, continuous until ROSC; mechanical CPR for prolonged rescue or transport
Continue BLS and ALS until the temperature is back to normal; consider stopping ECPR if there is no ROSC at the target temperature

orders.item: Intermittent CPR, only if continuous CPR is impossible
orders.dose: Core under 28 °C or unknown: at least 5 minutes of CPR, then at most 5 minutes without; under 20 °C, at most 10 minutes without

orders.note: The Korean 2025 guideline performs BLS and ALS by the standard guidelines in hypothermic arrest, and states no shock limit.

nodes.summary: Hypothermic cardiac arrest with no sign of irreversible death: continuous CPR to an ECLS centre for VA ECMO rewarming, with the HOPE score (10% or more favors ECLS) and clinical judgment guiding the decision. Rewarm at 5 °C/h or less; after ROSC, targeted temperature management by local protocol and no post-resuscitation hyperthermia. ECPR is stopped if there is no ROSC at the target temperature, or for uncontrollable bleeding or severe anoxic brain injury.

Hypothermic arrest with fixed dependent lividity, an injury incompatible with life or a valid DNR order: resuscitation is withheld or stopped. Stiff limbs alone are not one of these signs in Paal 2022, because apparent rigor mortis is unreliable in hypothermia; the Korean 2025 guideline still lists rigor mortis as a reason to stop. A HOPE estimate under 10% argues against ECLS rewarming.

nodes.ask: Pulled from the water: not breathing, no pulse, core 30 °C or more. Next?
options: Open the airway, give 5 rescue breaths, then CPR with ventilations and oxygen
Compression-only CPR at once, since breaths only delay the chest compressions
Abdominal thrusts first to drain water from the lungs, then start the CPR
A collar and spinal board before any breaths, then CPR in line with the spine
nodes.chainStep: Open the airway and give 5 rescue breaths, then chest compressions with ventilations and oxygen as soon as available; attach the AED once CPR is under way, without interrupting breaths and compressions; intubate if airway protection is inadequate (no supraglottic airway); spinal immobilization only for a dive, a fall or signs of trauma; remove wet clothing; ECMO as salvage for refractory hypoxemia or severe hypothermia
nodes.why: Hypoxia causes the arrest in drowning and drives the brain injury, so airway and breathing come before compressions: 5 initial rescue breaths rather than the usual 2. Compression-only CPR leaves out the treatment the patient needs, and the Heimlich maneuver is no longer recommended. Shockable rhythms are uncommon (2 to 12%), so the AED must not delay breaths and compressions. Spinal immobilization is only for a history or signs of trauma, such as a dive or a fall, so that it does not hold up the airway.

orders.dose: 5 initial breaths before compressions
No longer recommended in drowning
Shockable rhythms in only 2 to 12%; use it once CPR is under way, without delaying breaths or compressions
Not recommended in drowning: less reliable protection, more aspiration
When airway protection is inadequate or SpO2 stays under 90% despite high-flow oxygen
Immobilize only with a history or signs of trauma, such as a dive or a fall

nodes.summary: Drowning arrest: ventilation first (5 rescue breaths), then CPR with oxygen, intubation when airway protection is inadequate, and ECMO as salvage for refractory hypoxemia or severe hypothermia. Submersion time is the strongest predictor of survival, with mortality rising steeply beyond 5 minutes. A core under 30 °C makes this a hypothermic arrest (this pathway's hypothermic arrest route).

Cardiac arrest with a core of 30 °C or more, not after submersion (heat, an electrical injury, lightning, a bite, a dive, or cold that does not explain it): standard BLS and ALS, once the scene is safe from any current, with a search for the cause, since hypothermia alone does not explain an arrest above 30 °C. After lightning the pulse often returns before breathing does, so ventilation is supported early, the cervical spine is protected, and with several victims those in cardiac or respiratory arrest are treated first (reverse triage), because survivors of the strike rarely die later.

nodes.chainStep: Rectal (or esophageal) temperature and a mental status check at once; out of the heat, excess clothing off, cooling started; fingerstick glucose; CBC, PT and aPTT, metabolic panel with creatinine and liver tests, blood gas, CK, urine myoglobin, ECG; medication and drug review (diuretics, beta blockers, anticholinergics, antipsychotics, serotonergic drugs, stimulants, recent anesthesia)
nodes.why: Two findings sort heat illness: the core temperature and the brain. Heat stroke is central nervous system dysfunction (delirium, ataxia, seizures) with a core temperature typically, but not always, over 40 °C, and only a rectal or esophageal reading is valid; a falsely low tympanic reading delays the one treatment shown to cut mortality, rapid cooling. Antipyretics have no role. CT is for a presentation that does not fit, not a reason to hold cooling. The drug list matters: diuretics, beta blockers and anticholinergics predispose to classic heat stroke, and rigidity or clonus points to a drug-induced syndrome instead.

CBC, metabolic panel, PT and aPTT, blood gas, CK and urine myoglobin; glucose

nodes.chainStep: Cold-water immersion (stirred ice water, trunk and limbs up to the neck) where feasible; otherwise evaporative cooling (cool water mist and fans) with ice packs to groin, axillae and neck; continuous rectal or esophageal temperature; stop active cooling at 38 to 39 °C; aim to get under 38.9 °C within 30 minutes of collapse; IV access and rehydration, avoiding rapid sodium correction; benzodiazepine only for agitation or shivering; no antipyretics, no dantrolene; repeat CK, potassium, creatinine, liver tests, platelets and coagulation
nodes.why: Rapid cooling is the intervention that lowers mortality, and the time above the critical temperature drives the damage, so cooling starts at once and transport comes second. Cold-water immersion cools fastest and is the standard for exertional heat stroke; in older patients with classic heat stroke it can be impractical because monitoring is hard and agitation interferes, and evaporative cooling with mist and fans plus ice packs is the next option. Cooling stops near 39 °C to avoid overcooling. Antipyretics have no role in heat stroke and may harm the liver, and dantrolene has not improved outcomes.

nodes.summary: Heat stroke cooled quickly and recovering. Exertional: many cooled within 30 minutes go home the same day; return to activity only after a 7 to 21 day rest, normal blood work and physician clearance, then a graded progression. Classic heat stroke in an older patient: review the drugs that impair heat loss (diuretics, beta blockers, anticholinergics) and the home conditions before discharge; air conditioning, fluids and limiting daytime exposure prevent the next episode.

Heat stroke with organ injury: intensive care, fluids for rhabdomyolysis titrated to urine output, potassium treated as an emergency (pw_electrolytes), and blood products for DIC by bleeding and labs. Hypotension, a low GCS, a raised creatinine and DIC on admission carry the highest mortality; intravascular cooling, anticoagulation and blood purification are unproven.

Hyperthermia driven by a drug rather than the environment: rigidity and clonus are not features of heat stroke, and cooling is only an adjunct here. Serotonin toxicity and sympathomimetic toxicity follow the toxicology pathway (pw_tox), with benzodiazepines, supportive care and active cooling. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome continues in the agitation pathway (pw_agitation): every dopamine blocker stopped, ICU, aggressive cooling, fluids and electrolytes, and bromocriptine or dantrolene in severe cases. Malignant hyperthermia after a volatile anesthetic or succinylcholine: stop the trigger, 100% oxygen, IV dantrolene, active cooling and at least 24 hours of ICU care. No other pathway covers malignant hyperthermia yet.

nodes.ask: Core temperature under 35 °C. Next?
options: Handle gently and keep flat; stage by core and consciousness; ECG; look for a cause
Sit them up and get them walking now, and stage the cold by whether they shiver
Warm IV fluids alone, since they rewarm the core faster than any of the external methods

nodes.chainStep: Keep horizontal and handle gently; remove wet clothing and insulate; continuous core temperature on a low-reading probe; defibrillation pads and 12-lead ECG; fingerstick glucose, CBC, metabolic panel, fibrinogen, CK, lactate, TSH, cortisol and toxicology as indicated; stage: mild 32 to 35 °C, moderate 28 to 32 °C, severe under 28 °C (the Revised Swiss System uses consciousness when no core reading is available); look for sepsis, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, hypoglycemia, intoxication, trauma or stroke
nodes.why: Rough handling can trigger fatal dysrhythmias in moderate or severe hypothermia (rescue collapse), and a patient found lying down is not walked until fed and allowed to shiver for about 30 minutes. Shivering is not a consistent sign and is not used to stage hypothermia: staging comes from the core temperature and the level of consciousness. Warmed IV fluids stop further heat loss and treat volume depletion but rewarm only modestly. The ECG shows Osborn (J) waves, slowed conduction and often atrial fibrillation. Hypothermia out of proportion to the exposure points to another cause, such as sepsis, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, hypoglycemia or a drug.

Failure to rewarm (a static or falling core, rising lactate, falling consciousness or pressure, or a ventricular dysrhythmia) moves to active internal rewarming. In ICE-CRASH, ECMO helped hypothermic patients in arrest but not those with a pulse, in whom it added bleeding. Lavage is for severe cases when less invasive methods fail, and heat packs must not touch the skin, to prevent burns.

The slow pulse and low pressure are responses to the cold and need nothing beyond rewarming, not atropine or pacing. When the airway needs it, rapid-sequence intubation in a warm room is used: the arrhythmia risk is small next to the benefit.

nodes.chainStep: Correct moderate or severe hypothermia first; if still frozen, rapid rewarming in circulating water at 37 to 39 °C for about 30 minutes, until the tissue is soft and pliable, with analgesia; no rubbing and no refreezing; dry without rubbing, dry dressing, elevate; ibuprofen 12 mg/kg/day in 2 doses (maximum 2,400 mg/day in 4 doses); tetanus updated; drain clear or cloudy blisters, leave hemorrhagic blisters intact; aloe vera with dressing changes every 6 hours; no prophylactic antibiotics; oxygen if SpO2 under 88% or above 4,000 m
nodes.why: Once refreezing can be prevented, rapid rewarming in warm water until the tissue is soft and pliable is the standard; repeated thawing and refreezing does more harm. Passive thawing is the fallback only when active rewarming cannot be done, and vigorous rubbing adds tissue damage. Ibuprofen is given for its antiprostaglandin effect. The first appearance underestimates the injury, so debridement and amputation wait for demarcation, 1 to 3 months later, unless wet gangrene or sepsis forces it.

nodes.ask: Deep frostbite, no perfusion after rewarming, within 72 hours. Next?

Tourniquets, incision and suction, ice and pressure immobilization do not help, and prophylactic antibiotics and fasciotomy are avoided; antivenom is what lowers compartment pressures. Opioids are preferred to NSAIDs because the patient may become thrombocytopenic.

nodes.why: Decompression illness, whether decompression sickness or arterial gas embolism, is treated with recompression, and until then with oxygen as close to 100% as possible. A horizontal position is encouraged; head-down and left lateral positions are no longer recommended because they raise the risk of cerebral edema. Fluids should not contain glucose. An untreated pneumothorax is an absolute contraindication to hyperbaric treatment, so the chest film comes first. Aspirin and steroids lack supporting evidence, waiting a day loses the window in which recompression works best, and an unpressurized aircraft must stay under 300 m.
